requirements.requirement: /tmp mounted with noexec, nosuid, nodev on node1
requirements.summary: fstab entry added (tmpfs /tmp tmpfs defaults,nosuid,noexec,nodev), applied live via mount, findmnt confirmed rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec, and a functional test (chmod +x script) failed with Permission denied/exit 126, directly proving noexec enforcement.

requirements.requirement: /dev/shm mounted with noexec, nosuid, nodev on node1
requirements.summary: fstab entry added for /dev/shm with defaults,nosuid,noexec,nodev; remount applied live; findmnt/mount output confirmed rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec, upgrading from the baseline (nosuid,nodev only, no noexec).

requirements.requirement: Hardened mount options for /tmp and /dev/shm survive a reboot
requirements.summary: Pre-reboot boot_id and healthy state captured, reboot triggered and acknowledged, post-reboot boot_id differs (proving an actual restart), and post-reboot findmnt/mount output plus a repeated functional exec-block test (exit 126) confirm both mounts retained nosuid,nodev,noexec after the restart, with systemctl is-system-running reporting 'running'.

overall_summary: All three material outcomes — noexec/nosuid/nodev on /tmp, the same on /dev/shm, and persistence across a reboot — are directly demonstrated with live mount inspection, functional exec-block tests, and a full pre/post-reboot boot-identity transition showing the hardening survived intact. The node-restart evidence protocol was executed cleanly: healthy pre-restart baseline, restart acknowledgement, changed boot_id, and recovered service/mount state. Only a trivial leftover test file (/tmp/t2.sh) was left as minor residue.
limitations: The /tmp/t2.sh file created during post-reboot functional verification was not cleaned up, though it is inert (tmpfs, noexec enforced) and poses no functional risk.
No prepare phase was configured (prepare_enabled=false), so before-prepare and after-prepare snapshots are identical; this is expected and not a gap in executor evidence.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor commands were tightly scoped to the task: baseline inspection, fstab backup (sudo cp /etc/fstab /etc/fstab.bak.*), fstab edit, live remount, and functional verification before and after a bounded reboot. One command (cmd-29513a4a9f8b4c1e, an unprivileged cp attempt) failed with Permission denied and caused no state change; it was immediately corrected with sudo and is not a hygiene concern. The only residue is a trivial leftover verification script /tmp/t2.sh created after reboot (visible in after_executor temporary-files diff) — bounded, non-executable-by-design (tmpfs is noexec), and low risk, but it was not cleaned up. The fstab.bak backup file is an intentional, reasonable safety artifact, not penalized. No failed services, no unsafe exposure, no package damage were observed (failed-services and listening-sockets both empty before and after; package-health unchanged).
